title: Catch a ball flying out of a chute in a basket before it touches the table
instruction: In a few seconds a ball will fly out of the end of the covered chute. Catch it in the blue basket before it touches the table.
context: Parts leaving a chute or a feeder outlet have to land in a container, not on the bench, where they get damaged or roll off onto the floor; when the bin has been moved aside, someone has to get it under the outlet, where the part will come down rather than right below the outlet, before the next part comes out. The robot can't touch the ball first: it can only predict where it lands and be there in time.
setup: The two arm bases stand 61 cm apart on an oak table (1.10 x 1.30 m), whose left edge is 65 cm to the robot's left of the midpoint between the bases. A grey wooden chute runs along a line 34 cm in front of the bases, sloping down toward the left at 10 degrees: a floor board 36 cm long, 7.4 cm wide and 1.2 cm thick, with two dark side rails (6 mm wide, 6.2 cm tall, 6.2 cm apart inside) along its full length and a dark cover (6 mm thick, as wide as the chute) lying on the rails over its lower 24.9 cm. The board's lower end is open, its top surface there 15 cm above the table and 20 cm left of the midpoint; its upper end is 21.3 cm above the table, 15.5 cm right of the midpoint. Two wooden legs (6 cm across the chute's line, 3 cm along it) stand on the table under the board, reaching its underside: one 6 cm up the slope from the lower end (14.8 cm tall), one 32 cm up (19.3 cm tall). An orange rubber ball (5 cm diameter, 50 g) rests on the board's centre line in the uncovered top part, its contact point 30 cm up the slope from the lower end, against a grey gate (a 5.8 x 1 x 5.5 cm plate standing across the channel, 2 mm above the board). A blue plastic basket (an open box, 12.6 x 17.6 cm outside, 11 x 16 cm inside, 6.5 cm tall, 8 mm walls and floor, 100 g) stands on the table square to it, its long sides along the chute's line, its centre 20 cm in front of the bases and 52 cm left of the midpoint. A handle block (3 cm thick, 6 cm wide, 8 cm tall) stands up from the middle of its wall nearest the arms, rising 6 cm above the rim. Nothing else is on the table. At 7.5 s into the trial the gate lifts 8 cm straight up in 0.3 s and the ball rolls down inside the covered chute.
scoring: The trial counts what the ball does after the gate lifts. 1.0 if it is caught and then lies still for 1 s in the basket: caught means its centre is inside the basket's walls and below its rim, with the basket tilted at most 30 degrees, within 1 s after the ball was last inside the covered part of the chute, and before the ball touched the table (its underside within 3 mm of the table top, outside the basket's footprint). Otherwise, at the end of the trial: 0.75 if it was caught but did not stay; 0.5 if it came out of the chute's lower end and is inside the upright basket at the end (it touched the table or got there later than 1 s); 0.25 if it came out of the chute's lower end and has not gone over an edge of the table (its centre 5 cm or more below the table top); otherwise 0 (it is still in the chute, it never went through the chute, or it fell off the table).
reset_notes: Lower the gate, put the ball back against it on the chute's centre line and the basket back on its start spot; lift the gate 7.5 s after the trial starts. Catch the ball under the left edge if it falls.
fidelity: The chute, its cover and legs are fixed boxes; the gate follows its path exactly (it can't be pushed), like a solenoid gate. The ball is a rigid sphere with rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), no bounce and no rolling resistance: it leaves the chute at about 0.85 m/s and lands 13 cm past its end about 0.16 s later; a real rubber ball bounces a little in the basket and slows slightly on the table. The basket is one rigid body of box-shaped walls, floor and handle.
